raw: Act 1, Scene 5 — A Hall in Capulet’s House
Musicians waiting. Enter Servants.

sentences.en: Musicians are waiting.
Servants enter.

speaker: FIRST SERVANT
raw:
Where’s Potpan, that he helps not to take away?
He shift a trencher! He scrape a trencher!

sentences.en: Where is Potpan?
Why is he not helping to clear the tables?
Him, carry a plate? Him, scrape a plate? Never!

speaker: SECOND SERVANT
raw:
When good manners shall lie all in one or two men’s hands, and they
unwash’d too, ’tis a foul thing.

sentences.en: It is a bad thing when one or two men have all the good manners.
It is also bad if they do not wash their hands.

speaker: FIRST SERVANT
raw:
Away with the join-stools, remove the court-cupboard, look to the
plate. Good thou, save me a piece of marchpane; and as thou loves me,
let the porter let in Susan Grindstone and Nell. Antony and Potpan!

sentences.en: Take away the small stools and move the sideboard.
Watch the plates.
Please save a piece of marzipan for me.
If you love me, tell the doorman to let in Susan Grindstone and Nell.
Antony and Potpan!

speaker: SECOND SERVANT
raw: Ay, boy, ready.

sentences.en: Yes, boy, I am ready.

speaker: FIRST SERVANT
raw:
You are looked for and called for, asked for and sought for, in the
great chamber.

sentences.en: You are expected and called for.
People are asking for you.
They are looking for you in the great chamber.

speaker: SECOND SERVANT
raw:
We cannot be here and there too. Cheerly, boys. Be brisk awhile, and
the longer liver take all.

sentences.en: We cannot be in two places at once.
Hurry up, boys.
Be quick for a while.
The person who lives longest should take all.

raw: Exeunt.
Enter Capulet, &c. with the Guests and Gentlewomen to the Maskers.

sentences.en: Capulet enters with the guests and ladies.
They greet the masked guests.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
Welcome, gentlemen, ladies that have their toes
Unplagu’d with corns will have a bout with you.
Ah my mistresses, which of you all
Will now deny to dance? She that makes dainty,
She I’ll swear hath corns. Am I come near ye now?
Welcome, gentlemen! I have seen the day
That I have worn a visor, and could tell
A whispering tale in a fair lady’s ear,
Such as would please; ’tis gone, ’tis gone, ’tis gone,
You are welcome, gentlemen! Come, musicians, play.
A hall, a hall, give room! And foot it, girls.

sentences.en: Welcome, gentlemen.
Ladies, if your feet are healthy, you can dance with the men.
My dear ladies, which of you will refuse to dance?
If a lady acts shy, I swear she has painful feet.
Have I hit a sore spot?
Welcome, gentlemen!
I remember the day I wore a mask.
I could whisper a pleasant story into a beautiful lady's ear.
That time is gone, it is gone, it is gone.
You are welcome, gentlemen!
Come, musicians, play.
Clear the hall and give us room!
Dance now, girls.

raw: Music plays, and they dance.

sentences.en: Music plays and they dance.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
More light, you knaves; and turn the tables up,
And quench the fire, the room is grown too hot.
Ah sirrah, this unlook’d-for sport comes well.
Nay sit, nay sit, good cousin Capulet,
For you and I are past our dancing days;
How long is’t now since last yourself and I
Were in a mask?

sentences.en: Give me more light, you servants.
Fold up the tables.
Put out the fire because the room is too hot.
You there, this surprise party turned out well.
No, sit down, sit down, dear cousin Capulet.
You and I are past our dancing days.
How long has it been since we both wore masks?

speaker: CAPULET'S COUSIN
raw: By’r Lady, thirty years.

sentences.en: By the Virgin Mary, thirty years.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
What, man, ’tis not so much, ’tis not so much:
’Tis since the nuptial of Lucentio,
Come Pentecost as quickly as it will,
Some five and twenty years; and then we mask’d.

sentences.en: No, man, it is not that long.
It has been since Lucentio's wedding.
When the Pentecost holiday comes, it will be about twenty-five years.
We wore masks then.

speaker: CAPULET'S COUSIN
raw:
’Tis more, ’tis more, his son is elder, sir;
His son is thirty.

sentences.en: It is more, it is more.
His son is older, sir, because his son is thirty.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
Will you tell me that?
His son was but a ward two years ago.

sentences.en: Will you tell me that?
His son was still a child under a guardian two years ago.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
What lady is that, which doth enrich the hand
Of yonder knight?

sentences.en: What lady is that, dancing with that knight over there?

speaker: SERVANT
raw: I know not, sir.

sentences.en: I do not know, sir.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright!
It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night
As a rich jewel in an Ethiop’s ear;
Beauty too rich for use, for earth too dear!
So shows a snowy dove trooping with crows
As yonder lady o’er her fellows shows.
The measure done, I’ll watch her place of stand,
And touching hers, make blessed my rude hand.
Did my heart love till now? Forswear it, sight!
For I ne’er saw true beauty till this night.

sentences.en: Oh, she teaches the torches to burn bright!
She seems to hang on the cheek of night.
She looks like a rich jewel in an Ethiopian's ear.
Her beauty is too great for use.
It is too precious for this earth!
She stands out from the other ladies like a white dove among crows.
When the music ends, I will watch where she stands.
I will touch her hand.
I will make my rough hand blessed by her touch.
Did my heart love before now?
Deny it, sight!
I never saw true beauty until tonight.

speaker: TYBALT
raw:
This by his voice, should be a Montague.
Fetch me my rapier, boy. What, dares the slave
Come hither, cover’d with an antic face,
To fleer and scorn at our solemnity?
Now by the stock and honour of my kin,
To strike him dead I hold it not a sin.

sentences.en: By his voice, he must be a Montague.
Get me my thin sword, boy.
Does the slave dare to come here?
He is wearing a mask.
He comes to mock and insult our celebration.
I swear by my family's honor.
I do not think it is a sin to strike him dead.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
Why how now, kinsman!
Wherefore storm you so?

sentences.en: Why are you shouting, relative?
Why are you so angry?

speaker: TYBALT

sentences.en: Uncle, this is a Montague.
He is our enemy.
He is a villain who came here to cause trouble.
He comes to mock our ceremony tonight.

speaker: CAPULET
raw: Young Romeo, is it?

sentences.en: Young Romeo, is it?

speaker: TYBALT
raw: ’Tis he, that villain Romeo.

sentences.en: It is him, that villain Romeo.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
Content thee, gentle coz, let him alone,
A bears him like a portly gentleman;
And, to say truth, Verona brags of him
To be a virtuous and well-govern’d youth.
I would not for the wealth of all the town
Here in my house do him disparagement.
Therefore be patient, take no note of him,
It is my will; the which if thou respect,
Show a fair presence and put off these frowns,
An ill-beseeming semblance for a feast.

sentences.en: Be calm, my dear relative, and leave him alone.
He behaves like a well-mannered gentleman.
To tell the truth, Verona praises him as a virtuous and well-behaved youth.
I would not insult him in my house for all the wealth of the town.
Therefore be patient and do not pay him any attention.
That is my wish.
If you follow my wish, show a pleasant face.
Stop making these faces because they do not look good for a feast.

speaker: TYBALT
raw:
It fits when such a villain is a guest:
I’ll not endure him.

sentences.en: These frowns fit when such a villain is a guest.
I will not tolerate him.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
He shall be endur’d.
What, goodman boy! I say he shall, go to;
Am I the master here, or you? Go to.
You’ll not endure him! God shall mend my soul,
You’ll make a mutiny among my guests!
You will set cock-a-hoop, you’ll be the man!

sentences.en: He shall be tolerated.
What, boy! I say he shall. Enough!
Am I the master here, or are you?
Enough!
You will not tolerate him!
God save my soul, you will start a riot among my guests!
You will make trouble.
You want to play the big man!

speaker: TYBALT
raw: Why, uncle, ’tis a shame.

sentences.en: Well, uncle, it is a shame.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
Go to, go to!
You are a saucy boy. Is’t so, indeed?
This trick may chance to scathe you, I know what.
You must contrary me! Marry, ’tis time.
Well said, my hearts!—You are a princox; go:
Be quiet, or—More light, more light!—For shame!
I’ll make you quiet. What, cheerly, my hearts.

sentences.en: Enough, enough! You are a rude boy.
Is that so? This behavior might hurt you, I know it.
You must disagree with me, but it is time you learned!
Well said, my friends! You are a bold boy; go.
Be quiet, or—More light, more light!
Shame on you! I will make you quiet.
Cheer up, my friends!

speaker: TYBALT
raw:
Patience perforce with wilful choler meeting
Makes my flesh tremble in their different greeting.
I will withdraw: but this intrusion shall,
Now seeming sweet, convert to bitter gall.

sentences.en: Forced patience meeting my strong anger makes me shake.
I will leave now.
But this intrusion will seem sweet now.
It will turn into bitter poison later.

raw: Exit.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
If I profane with my unworthiest hand
This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this,
My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand
To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.

sentences.en: If I make this holy shrine dirty with my unworthy hand, the gentle sin is this.
My lips are like two blushing pilgrims, travelers to a holy place.
They are ready to smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
Which mannerly devotion shows in this;
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch,
And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss.

sentences.en: Good pilgrim, you blame your hand too much.
This shows a polite devotion.
Saints have hands that pilgrims' hands touch.
And palm to palm is the holy kiss of pilgrims.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Have not saints lips, and holy palmers too?

sentences.en: Do not saints have lips?
And do holy pilgrims not have lips too?

speaker: JULIET
raw: Ay, pilgrim, lips that they must use in prayer.

sentences.en: Yes, pilgrim.
They must use their lips in prayer.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
O, then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do:
They pray, grant thou, lest faith turn to despair.

sentences.en: Then, dear saint, let your lips do what hands do.
They pray, so please grant this.
Otherwise faith will turn to despair.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Saints do not move, though grant for prayers’ sake.

sentences.en: Saints do not move, even when they grant prayers.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Then move not while my prayer’s effect I take.
Thus from my lips, by thine my sin is purg’d.

sentences.en: Then do not move while I receive the effect of my prayer.
So your lips wash the sin from my lips.

raw: Kissing her.

sentences.en: Romeo kisses her.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Then have my lips the sin that they have took.

sentences.en: Then my lips have the sin that they took.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Sin from my lips? O trespass sweetly urg’d!
Give me my sin again.

sentences.en: Sin from my lips? Oh, this is a sweet crime, so give me my sin again.

speaker: JULIET
raw: You kiss by the book.

sentences.en: You kiss according to the rules.

speaker: NURSE
raw: Madam, your mother craves a word with you.

sentences.en: Madam, your mother wants to speak with you.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: What is her mother?

sentences.en: Who is her mother?

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Marry, bachelor,
Her mother is the lady of the house,
And a good lady, and a wise and virtuous.
I nurs’d her daughter that you talk’d withal.
I tell you, he that can lay hold of her
Shall have the chinks.

sentences.en: Well, young man.
Her mother is the lady of the house.
She is a good lady.
She is wise and virtuous.
I nursed the daughter that you are talking about.
I tell you, the man who can win her will get lots of money.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Is she a Capulet?
O dear account! My life is my foe’s debt.

sentences.en: Is she a Capulet?
Oh, what a costly thing to learn!
My life is now in my enemy's hands.

speaker: BENVOLIO
raw: Away, be gone; the sport is at the best.

sentences.en: Come, let us go.
The fun is at its best, so it is a good time to leave.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Ay, so I fear; the more is my unrest.

sentences.en: Yes, I fear that.
It makes me more uneasy.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
Nay, gentlemen, prepare not to be gone,
We have a trifling foolish banquet towards.
Is it e’en so? Why then, I thank you all;
I thank you, honest gentlemen; good night.
More torches here! Come on then, let’s to bed.
Ah, sirrah, by my fay, it waxes late,
I’ll to my rest.

sentences.en: No, gentlemen, do not get ready to leave because we have a small and silly banquet ahead.
Is it really so? Then I thank you all and I thank you, honest gentlemen.
Good night. Bring more torches here!
Come on then, let us go to bed.
Ah, you there, by my faith, it is getting late, so I will go to my rest.

raw: Exeunt all but Juliet and Nurse.

sentences.en: Everyone leaves except Juliet and the Nurse.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Come hither, Nurse. What is yond gentleman?

sentences.en: Come here, Nurse.
Who is that gentleman over there?

speaker: NURSE
raw: The son and heir of old Tiberio.

sentences.en: He is the son and heir of old Tiberio.

speaker: JULIET
raw: What’s he that now is going out of door?

sentences.en: Who is that man going out of the door now?

speaker: NURSE
raw: Marry, that I think be young Petruchio.

sentences.en: I think that is young Petruchio.

speaker: JULIET
raw: What’s he that follows here, that would not dance?

sentences.en: Who is that man following here who does not want to dance?

speaker: NURSE
raw: I know not.

sentences.en: I do not know.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Go ask his name. If he be married,
My grave is like to be my wedding bed.

sentences.en: Go and ask his name.
If he is married, my grave will be like my wedding bed.

speaker: NURSE
raw:
His name is Romeo, and a Montague,
The only son of your great enemy.

sentences.en: His name is Romeo.
He is a Montague.
He is the only son of your great enemy.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
My only love sprung from my only hate!
Too early seen unknown, and known too late!
Prodigious birth of love it is to me,
That I must love a loathed enemy.

sentences.en: My only love comes from my only hate!
I saw him too early as a stranger.
I know him too late now.
It is a strange and frightening birth of love.
I must love an enemy that I hate.

speaker: NURSE
raw: What’s this? What’s this?

sentences.en: What is this?
What is this?

speaker: JULIET
raw:
A rhyme I learn’d even now
Of one I danc’d withal.

sentences.en: I just learned a rhyme now.
It is about the man I danced with.

raw: One calls within, ‘Juliet’.

sentences.en: Someone calls from inside for Juliet.

speaker: NURSE
raw:
Anon, anon!
Come let’s away, the strangers all are gone.

sentences.en: Coming, coming! Come, let us go away because all the strangers are gone.

raw: Exeunt.
